For CGT purposes, the s.62(6) election treats the variation as a disposal by the deceased's executors rather than by the beneficiary, preserving the s.62(1) death-uplift. The combined route is one of the most powerful post-death rescue tools: a surviving spouse who inherits the BTL portfolio outright can redirect some or all of it into an IPDI for themselves with remainder to children, achieving the IPDI's control and ring-fencing benefits without losing the first-death spouse exemption or the death-uplift CGT base cost. For the deed-of-variation depth, see our guide to deeds of variation on landlord estates."
- Before: answer: "The RNRB is available on the second death where the residence passes to lineal descendants. For the spouse-IPDI structure on a rental portfolio (not the main home), the RNRB is available against the main home on second death if the main home passes to children (under the spouse's own will), but is NOT directly available against the rental portfolio (the RNRB applies only to a 'qualifying residential interest' which means a residence the deceased lived in at some point). The portfolio's IHT is at the standard 40% rate above NRB. Where the second-death estate exceeds £2m, the RNRB tapers by £1 for every £2 over the threshold, fully withdrawn at £2.7m for a single RNRB or £3.05m for the combined own-plus-transferred RNRB. For substantial portfolios that push the second-death estate above £2.7m even after the spouse-IPDI structure, RNRB is fully tapered; the second-death IHT cost is at the full 40% rate. Strategic planning options to reduce the second-death taper exposure include: charitable legacies under IHTA 1984 Sch 1A (reduced 36% rate where 10% of net estate left to charity); BPR-qualifying business assets (out of the £2m taper calculation entirely); and pension-fund preservation (pension funds outside the estate for IHT purposes until April 2027, then partially within). For the RNRB taper depth treatment, see our Wave 2 A8 page on RNRB."
  After: answer: "The RNRB is available on the second death where the residence passes to lineal descendants. For the spouse-IPDI structure on a rental portfolio (not the main home), the RNRB is available against the main home on second death if the main home passes to children (under the spouse's own will), but is NOT directly available against the rental portfolio (the RNRB applies only to a 'qualifying residential interest' which means a residence the deceased lived in at some point). The portfolio's IHT is at the standard 40% rate above NRB. For the RNRB taper depth treatment, see our guide to the RNRB £2m taper on property portfolios."
- Before: answer: "On the testator's death, the executors administer the estate, identify the IPDI trust property, value it at MV at death (for both IHT and CGT base-cost purposes), and transfer it to the trustees of the IPDI trust. The IPDI starts on the date the trustees become the legal owners. From that date the trustees administer the trust: collect rents, pay trust expenses, distribute net income to the IPDI holder, maintain trust accounts and SA returns. The trustees may be the same persons as the executors (with appropriate hat-changes in the documentation) or different persons. For property cases the trustees are typically a mix of family members and a professional trustee (typically a solicitor or accountant). The IPDI trustees should register the trust with the Trust Registration Service within 90 days of trust creation if the trust has any UK tax liability. Annual TRS updates are required. For the executor walkthrough on inheriting UK rental property in detail, see our existing Wave 2 A7 page on inheriting UK rental property executors step by step."
  After: answer: "On the testator's death, the executors administer the estate, identify the IPDI trust property, value it at MV at death (for both IHT and CGT base-cost purposes), and transfer it to the trustees of the IPDI trust. From that date the trustees administer the trust: collect rents, pay trust expenses, distribute net income to the IPDI holder, maintain trust accounts and SA returns. The trustees may be the same persons as the executors (with appropriate hat-changes in the documentation) or different persons. For property cases the trustees are typically a mix of family members and a professional trustee (typically a solicitor or accountant). The IPDI trustees should register the trust with the Trust Registration Service within 90 days of trust creation if the trust has any UK tax liability. Annual TRS updates are required. For the executor walkthrough on inheriting UK rental property in detail, see our step-by-step guide for executors inheriting UK rental property."

- Before: answer: "TMA 1970 s.12B requires self-employed and landlord taxpayers to retain records for at least five years from the 31 January submission deadline (six years from the end of the relevant tax year). House position §19.16 adopts a seven-year retention discipline as the practical floor, allowing margin for HMRC's discovery time limits (four years standard, six years for careless behaviour, twenty years for deliberate behaviour) and the inevitable late arrival of post-cessation paperwork. **Property/web/content/blog/mtd-itsa-joint-property-owners-quarterly-filing-mechanics-each-spouse.md**

- Before: answer: "Each owner records their share of the gross rent received (not the net), their share of agent commission, their share of management fees, and their share of any other deductions, all according to the beneficial-ownership split. The agent's statement is the source document; each owner extracts their share. A statement showing £4,000 gross rent, £400 agent commission, £150 management fee, £3,450 net paid to the joint account is recorded by each 50/50 spouse as £2,000 gross income, £200 commission expense, £75 management fee expense. Recording the £3,450 net as gross income would understate qualifying income for the threshold test (a known trap, covered in house position §19.13)."

Recording the £3,450 net as gross income would understate qualifying income for the threshold test (a known trap)."

The trap here is recording the net payment to the joint account as gross income, which understates the gross figure for the threshold test (covered in house position §19.13).

**Property/web/content/blog/mtd-itsa-pension-funds-sipp-ssas-holding-rental-property-treatment.md**

- Before: summary: "Landlords with a Self-Invested Personal Pension (SIPP) or Small Self-Administered Scheme (SSAS) holding commercial rental property arrive at Making Tax Digital with a recurring question: does the pension-held rental aggregate with my personal portfolio for the £50,000 threshold test, and do I file the pension property's quarterly updates inside MTD ITSA? Both answers are no. Pension trustees are outside MTD ITSA entirely under the §19.3 excluded categories, and the rental income within the pension wrapper is generally exempt from income tax inside a registered pension scheme. This page walks the trustee-exclusion mechanic, the SIPP-versus-SSAS distinction, the arm's-length rent discipline HMRC enforces via PTM121000, why residential property in a pension is the heavily restricted edge, the parallel-streams worked example (personal portfolio plus pension-held unit), and what changes when you start drawing pension income."
  After: summary: "Landlords with a Self-Invested Personal Pension (SIPP) or Small Self-Administered Scheme (SSAS) holding commercial rental property arrive at Making Tax Digital with a recurring question: does the pension-held rental aggregate with my personal portfolio for the £50,000 threshold test, and do I file the pension property's quarterly updates inside MTD ITSA? Both answers are no. Pension trustees are outside MTD ITSA entirely under the excluded categories, and the rental income within the pension wrapper is generally exempt from income tax inside a registered pension scheme. This page walks the trustee-exclusion mechanic, the SIPP-versus-SSAS distinction, the arm's-length rent discipline HMRC enforces via PTM121000, why residential property in a pension is the heavily restricted edge, the parallel-streams worked example (personal portfolio plus pension-held unit), and what changes when you start drawing pension income."
- Before: answer: "No. Rental income arising on property held inside a registered pension scheme (SIPP or SSAS) is income of the pension scheme, not of you the member. It does not appear on your personal self-assessment return as your rental income, and it does not feed the qualifying-income figure used for the MTD ITSA threshold test. House position §19.12 confirms this explicitly. A member with £40,000 of personal residential rents and a £35,000 SIPP-held commercial rent tests £40,000 only against the threshold, not £75,000."
  After: answer: "No. Rental income arising on property held inside a registered pension scheme (SIPP or SSAS) is income of the pension scheme, not of you the member. It does not appear on your personal self-assessment return as your rental income, and it does not feed the qualifying-income figure used for the MTD ITSA threshold test. That is our position. A member with £40,000 of personal residential rents and a £35,000 SIPP-held commercial rent tests £40,000 only against the threshold, not £75,000."
- Before: answer: "Nobody, in the MTD ITSA sense. Pension scheme trustees are not in scope for MTD ITSA at all (per the §19.3 excluded categories, MTD ITSA covers individuals and partnerships, not trustees of registered pension schemes). The scheme administrator (the SIPP provider or the SSAS practitioner) handles the scheme's own statutory reporting via the Pension Schemes Online service, the event report, and the registered pension scheme return where relevant. That is a separate regime from MTD ITSA and is not on a quarterly cycle."
  After: answer: "Nobody, in the MTD ITSA sense. Pension scheme trustees are not in scope for MTD ITSA at all (per the excluded categories, MTD ITSA covers individuals and partnerships, not trustees of registered pension schemes). The scheme administrator (the SIPP provider or the SSAS practitioner) handles the scheme's own statutory reporting via the Pension Schemes Online service, the event report, and the registered pension scheme return where relevant. That is a separate regime from MTD ITSA and is not on a quarterly cycle."

  After: reviewerCredentials: "UK-based tax advisers specialising in property income, MTD ITSA implementation, and the SIPP / SSAS commercial-property edge case."

House position §19.12 follows from §19.3: property income within the pension wrapper is taxed (or, more precisely, exempted from income tax) inside the scheme under Finance Act 2004 Part 4, reported via the scheme administrator's own statutory channel, and does not flow through the member's personal MTD ITSA cycle.

**Property/web/content/blog/mtd-itsa-spreadsheets-with-bridging-software-allowed-mechanics.md**

- Before: summary: "Landlords running on a longstanding spreadsheet often resist swapping to a full SaaS accounting suite for MTD ITSA, and they are right to ask whether they have to. The answer is no. House position §19.6 and §19.14 confirm that spreadsheet plus HMRC-recognised bridging software is a permitted route, provided every data transfer satisfies the digital-link rule. This page works the operational mechanics: what counts as a digital link and what does not (cell references and CSV exports yes, copy-paste no), what bridging software actually does between spreadsheet and HMRC API, the spreadsheet column discipline that maps to the SA105 expense categories, a worked compliant-versus-non-compliant data flow, and when the spreadsheet route is sensibly the right answer versus when a full SaaS suite saves the friction."
  After: summary: "Landlords running on a longstanding spreadsheet often resist swapping to a full SaaS accounting suite for MTD ITSA, and they are right to ask whether they have to. **Property/web/content/blog/putting-rental-property-into-a-trust-decision-pillar-iht-cgt-sdlt-stack.md**

- Before: answer: "A lifetime settlement of property into a discretionary trust is a chargeable lifetime transfer (CLT) under IHTA 1984, paying 20% entry IHT on the value above the settlor's available NRB. The trust then runs under the relevant property regime (s.64 10-year periodic charge up to 6%, s.65 exit charges on capital distributions). The strategic value is on the CGT side: TCGA 1992 s.260 allows the settlor and trustees to jointly elect to hold over the gain on the transfer in, deferring it into the trust's base cost. The s.260 election is conditional on the trust being non-settlor-interested (TCGA 1992 ss.169B to 169G; the settlor and the settlor's spouse must be expressly excluded from the beneficiary class). The route wins where: (a) the property has a substantial latent CGT gain (the £25,000-plus that would otherwise crystallise at 18% to 24% residential CGT under s.17 on the transfer in is deferred), (b) the family wants trustee-governance control with multi-generational distribution flexibility, (c) the family is comfortable with the £15,000-ish entry IHT cost on a typical £400,000 BTL with full unused NRB, and (d) the drafting can be done cleanly (express exclusion of settlor and spouse; covered in depth on our Wave 6 B4 page on the three-statute attribution stack). It loses where the trust is settlor-interested (CGT crystallises immediately, removing the strategic value)."
  After: answer: "A lifetime settlement of property into a discretionary trust is a chargeable lifetime transfer (CLT) under IHTA 1984, paying 20% entry IHT on the value above the settlor's available NRB. The trust then runs under the relevant property regime (s.64 10-year periodic charge up to 6%, s.65 exit charges on capital distributions). The strategic value is on the CGT side: TCGA 1992 s.260 allows the settlor and trustees to jointly elect to hold over the gain on the transfer in, deferring it into the trust's base cost. The s.260 election is conditional on the trust being non-settlor-interested (TCGA 1992 ss.169B to 169G; the settlor and the settlor's spouse must be expressly excluded from the beneficiary class). The route wins where: (a) the property has a substantial latent CGT gain (the £25,000-plus that would otherwise crystallise at 18% to 24% residential CGT under s.17 on the transfer in is deferred), (b) the family wants trustee-governance control with multi-generational distribution flexibility, (c) the family is comfortable with the £15,000-ish entry IHT cost on a typical £400,000 BTL with full unused NRB, and (d) the drafting can be done cleanly (express exclusion of settlor and spouse; covered in depth on our page on the three-statute attribution stack). It loses where the trust is settlor-interested (CGT crystallises immediately, removing the strategic value)."
- Before: answer: "A bare trust (also called a nominee arrangement) is one where the beneficiary has the exclusive right to direct the trustee how to deal with the property, subject only to satisfying any outstanding charge or lien. TCGA 1992 s.60 treats the bare trustee's acts in relation to the property as the acts of the beneficiary; transactions between the trustee and beneficiary are disregarded; the beneficiary is the direct owner for CGT purposes. For income tax, the same transparency applies: rental income from a bare-trust property is taxed on the beneficiary at their marginal rate. For IHT, the transfer into bare trust is a PET (potentially exempt transfer); the property is NOT in the relevant property regime (no 10-year periodic charges, no exit charges); the beneficiary is treated as the absolute owner from the gift date. Bare trusts win where: (a) the beneficiary is a minor and the family wants to start the IHT 7-year clock running immediately while retaining trustee control over actual day-to-day decisions until the child reaches 18, (b) the family wants the simplicity of full transparency (no trust tax returns at trust rates, no separate trust entity for IHT purposes), and (c) the s.629 ITTOIA 2005 income-tax attribution on minor-child distributions is acceptable (the income-tax outcome on a parent-to-minor-child bare-trust gift is the same as direct retention for income-tax purposes, but the IHT clock is running). Covered in depth on our forthcoming Wave 6 B6 page on bare trust vs nominee company vs formal trust."
  After: answer: "A bare trust (also called a nominee arrangement) is one where the beneficiary has the exclusive right to direct the trustee how to deal with the property, subject only to satisfying any outstanding charge or lien. TCGA 1992 s.60 treats the bare trustee's acts in relation to the property as the acts of the beneficiary; transactions between the trustee and beneficiary are disregarded; the beneficiary is the direct owner for CGT purposes. For income tax, the same transparency applies: rental income from a bare-trust property is taxed on the beneficiary at their marginal rate. For IHT, the transfer into bare trust is a PET (potentially exempt transfer); the property is NOT in the relevant property regime (no 10-year periodic charges, no exit charges); the beneficiary is treated as the absolute owner from the gift date. Bare trusts win where: (a) the beneficiary is a minor and the family wants to start the IHT 7-year clock running immediately while retaining trustee control over actual day-to-day decisions until the child reaches 18, (b) the family wants the simplicity of full transparency (no trust tax returns at trust rates, no separate trust entity for IHT purposes), and (c) the s.629 ITTOIA 2005 income-tax attribution on minor-child distributions is acceptable (the income-tax outcome on a parent-to-minor-child bare-trust gift is the same as direct retention for income-tax purposes, but the IHT clock is running). Covered in depth on our page on bare trust vs nominee company vs formal trust."
- Before: answer: "The bare trust route, in nearly all cases. The bare trust mechanism preserves the IHT-clock benefit (PET starts immediately from gift date; the property is outside the relevant property regime; the beneficiary is treated as the absolute owner from gift date) while keeping the trustees in legal control of the property until the child reaches 18 (or whatever age the deed specifies for transfer of legal title). The income-tax outcome via ITTOIA 2005 s.629 attribution (rents on the child's share of the property are taxed on the parent-settlor at the parent's marginal rate, subject to the £100 per-settlement de-minimis) is unavoidable on any parent-to-minor-child route; the bare trust is no worse on this front than direct transfer-of-title. The discretionary trust route loses heavily on parent-to-minor-child gifts because it adds the 20% entry IHT cost (the £325,000 NRB is shared across all the parent's CLTs in the seven-year cumulation window; multiple-property CLTs can quickly exhaust the NRB), the 10-year periodic charge, and the trust-rate income-tax rate. The grandparent-route variation (grandparent as settlor; s.629 attributes to grandparent rather than parent, often at a more favourable marginal rate) is a separate structural option covered on our Wave 6 B9 page on gifting property to minor children."
  After: answer: "The bare trust route, in nearly all cases. The bare trust mechanism preserves the IHT-clock benefit (PET starts immediately from gift date; the property is outside the relevant property regime; the beneficiary is treated as the absolute owner from gift date) while keeping the trustees in legal control of the property until the child reaches 18 (or whatever age the deed specifies for transfer of legal title). The income-tax outcome via ITTOIA 2005 s.629 attribution (rents on the child's share of the property are taxed on the parent-settlor at the parent's marginal rate, subject to the £100 per-settlement de-minimis) is unavoidable on any parent-to-minor-child route; the bare trust is no worse on this front than direct transfer-of-title. The discretionary trust route loses heavily on parent-to-minor-child gifts because it adds the 20% entry IHT cost (the £325,000 NRB is shared across all the parent's CLTs in the seven-year cumulation window; multiple-property CLTs can quickly exhaust the NRB), the 10-year periodic charge, and the trust-rate income-tax rate. The grandparent-route variation (grandparent as settlor; s.629 attributes to grandparent rather than parent, often at a more favourable marginal rate) is a separate structural option covered on our page on gifting property to minor children."
- Before: answer: "Five mistakes account for most of the value lost in the cluster. (1) Settlor-interested drafting on a discretionary trust: including the settlor or settlor's spouse in the beneficiary class breaks the s.260 holdover, triggers s.624 income-tax attribution, and crystallises CGT immediately. The fix is express exclusion in the deed (see our Wave 6 B4 page). (2) Gift-with-reservation on top of any property gift: the donor continues to occupy or take rents from the gifted property, triggering FA 1986 s.102, with the property added back to the death estate at MV at death (see our Wave 6 B7 page on the double-trap). (3) Failing to refinance the mortgage out before the transfer: leaving the mortgage in place and having the trustees assume it triggers FA 2003 Sch 4 para 8 SDLT on the assumed debt. The fix is pre-transfer refinance. (4) Misclassifying the trust type: drafting what was intended as a bare trust but with discretionary-class language, accidentally creating a discretionary trust subject to entry IHT and the relevant property regime. The fix is precision in the deed wording. (5) Not coordinating with the will: a lifetime trust plus a will that creates an IPDI for the surviving spouse on the same property can produce conflicting IHT-add-back consequences. The fix is integrated estate-planning that designs the lifetime structure and the will together as a single plan."
  After: answer: "Five mistakes account for most of the value lost in the cluster. (1) Settlor-interested drafting on a discretionary trust: including the settlor or settlor's spouse in the beneficiary class breaks the s.260 holdover, triggers s.624 income-tax attribution, and crystallises CGT immediately. The fix is express exclusion in the deed (see our page on the three-statute attribution stack). (2) Gift-with-reservation on top of any property gift: the donor continues to occupy or take rents from the gifted property, triggering FA 1986 s.102, with the property added back to the death estate at MV at death (see our page on the double-trap). (3) Failing to refinance the mortgage out before the transfer: leaving the mortgage in place and having the trustees assume it triggers FA 2003 Sch 4 para 8 SDLT on the assumed debt. The fix is pre-transfer refinance. (4) Misclassifying the trust type: drafting what was intended as a bare trust but with discretionary-class language, accidentally creating a discretionary trust subject to entry IHT and the relevant property regime. The fix is precision in the deed wording. (5) Not coordinating with the will: a lifetime trust plus a will that creates an IPDI for the surviving spouse on the same property can produce conflicting IHT-add-back consequences. The fix is integrated estate-planning that designs the lifetime structure and the will together as a single plan."
- Before: The three-tax stack runs across all four vehicles: IHT entry charge, CGT entry charge, and SDLT entry charge. The often-overlooked rule on the SDLT side is FA 2003 Schedule 4 paragraph 8, which treats assumed mortgage debt as chargeable consideration for SDLT regardless of whether any cash changes hands; this rule catches three of the four vehicles (the IPDI route is the only one that escapes, because death is not an SDLT event). Sessions across the Wave 6 B-cluster forward-link to this pillar for the four-vehicle framing.
  After: The three-tax stack runs across all four vehicles: IHT entry charge, CGT entry charge, and SDLT entry charge. - Before: The lifetime discretionary trust route is a CLT into the relevant property regime under IHTA 1984. Where the trust is clean (settlor and spouse expressly excluded from the beneficiary class; covered in depth on our Wave 6 B4 page on the three-statute attribution stack ), the route delivers £42,480 of CGT deferral on a typical £400,000 BTL with £180,000 latent gain in exchange for the £15,000 entry IHT cost; net Year 0 cost saving of £27,480 versus the bare-trust route or the FIC route.

- Before: IHT: IHTA 1984 s.49(1A). Verbatim s.49(1A): for IIPs arising on or after 22 March 2006, the s.49(1) read-through (treating the IIP holder as beneficially entitled to the underlying property for IHT) applies only where the IIP is an immediate-post-death interest (IPDI), a disabled person's interest, or a transitional serial interest, or falls within s.5(1B). The s.49(1A) mechanic is not itself an attribution rule in the same sense as s.624 or s.169B; it operates by carving certain post-2006 IIPs back into the s.49(1) treatment, with the effect that any IPDI for the settlor or settlor's spouse causes the property to sit in the IIP-holder's estate for IHT. Pairs in practice with the parallel FA 1986 s.102 gifts-with-reservation track, which is the substantive IHT add-back mechanism (covered on Wave 6 B5 and B7).
  After: IHT: IHTA 1984 s.49(1A). Verbatim s.49(1A): for IIPs arising on or after 22 March 2006, the s.49(1) read-through (treating the IIP holder as beneficially entitled to the underlying property for IHT) applies only where the IIP is an immediate-post-death interest (IPDI), a disabled person's interest, or a transitional serial interest, or falls within s.5(1B). The s.49(1A) mechanic is not itself an attribution rule in the same sense as s.624 or s.169B; it operates by carving certain post-2006 IIPs back into the s.49(1) treatment, with the effect that any IPDI for the settlor or settlor's spouse causes the property to sit in the IIP-holder's estate for IHT. Pairs in practice with the parallel FA 1986 s.102 gifts-with-reservation track, which is the substantive IHT add-back mechanism (covered on our family-home GROB and double-trap guides).

- Before: answer: "From 6 April 2027, property income in England, Wales and NI is taxed at 22% (basic), 42% (higher), 47% (additional) per FA 2026, enacted 18 March 2026 (HP §7, locked). The Section 24 reducer also rises to 22% in 2027/28. Key result: for basic-rate landlords, the reducer (22%) matches the property income rate (22%), so no new wedge opens at basic rate. For higher-rate landlords, the wedge remains at 20 percentage points (42% minus 22%) in 2027/28, the same as in 2026/27 (40% minus 20%). The case for incorporating does not weaken in 2027/28; the corporation tax rate (19% or 25% depending on profits) remains well below the 42% higher rate on rental income."
  After: answer: "From 6 April 2027, property income in England, Wales and NI is taxed at 22% (basic), 42% (higher), 47% (additional) per FA 2026, enacted 18 March 2026. The Section 24 reducer also rises to 22% in 2027/28. Key result: for basic-rate landlords, the reducer (22%) matches the property income rate (22%), so no new wedge opens at basic rate. For higher-rate landlords, the wedge remains at 20 percentage points (42% minus 22%) in 2027/28, the same as in 2026/27 (40% minus 20%). The case for incorporating does not weaken in 2027/28; the corporation tax rate (19% or 25% depending on profits) remains well below the 42% higher rate on rental income."
- Before: Under Section 24, you cannot deduct mortgage interest and finance costs from rental income to arrive at taxable profit. Instead, you pay income tax on the full rental income and then receive a basic-rate credit (20% of finance costs in 2026/27; 22% from 6 April 2027 under FA 2026, enacted 18 March 2026, HP §7). For a basic-rate taxpayer, the credit roughly offsets the tax cost of not deducting the interest. For a higher-rate taxpayer, the difference is irrecoverable.
  After: Under Section 24, you cannot deduct mortgage interest and finance costs from rental income to arrive at taxable profit. Instead, you pay income tax on the full rental income and then receive a basic-rate credit (20% of finance costs in 2026/27; 22% from 6 April 2027 under FA 2026, enacted 18 March 2026). For a basic-rate taxpayer, the credit roughly offsets the tax cost of not deducting the interest. For a higher-rate taxpayer, the difference is irrecoverable.

- Before: NRCGT applies whether or not the treaty assigns UK rights. Per house positions §16.3 and HMRC INTM151010, the UK NRCGT regime applies as a statutory matter and the treaty is consistent with this. Older treaties that lacked Article 13(4) (notably the pre-2018 legacy CD arrangements) did not assign UK rights; UK statute imposed NRCGT anyway; HMRC's position was that this was consistent with the treaty because the UK was exercising rights the treaty did not deny. The 2018 treaties have now caught up: the treaty itself assigns the rights.
  After: NRCGT applies whether or not the treaty assigns UK rights. Per HMRC INTM151010, the UK NRCGT regime applies as a statutory matter and the treaty is consistent with this. Older treaties that lacked Article 13(4) (notably the pre-2018 legacy CD arrangements) did not assign UK rights; UK statute imposed NRCGT anyway; HMRC's position was that this was consistent with the treaty because the UK was exercising rights the treaty did not deny. The 2018 treaties have now caught up: the treaty itself assigns the rights.

- Before: summary: "Where the standard partial-exemption method at SI 1995/2518 regulation 101 materially distorts a mixed-portfolio landlord's residual-input-tax recovery, three statutory levers operate: the special method approval route at regulation 102 (verbatim heading 'Use of other methods', prior HMRC approval required, written method, fair-and-reasonable declaration); the standard-method override at regulation 107A (verbatim heading 'Adjustment of attribution', inserted by SI 2002/1074 effective 18 April 2002, triggered where standard-method attribution differs substantially from actual use); and the HMRC direction route at regulation 102B (where HMRC requires a taxable person to use a special method). This page walks each route in depth, classifies the typical Proposed Special Methods (PESMs) approved for property portfolios (sectorised, floor-area, headcount, transaction-count), runs the Lansdowne Estates worked example showing a 12-percentage-point recovery uplift on a £400,000 residual cost base, and closes with the decision tree mapping portfolio shape to method choice. Companion to the Wave 5 standard-method page; the special-method route is what comes after standard method when standard method does not work."
  After: summary: "Where the standard partial-exemption method at SI 1995/2518 regulation 101 materially distorts a mixed-portfolio landlord's residual-input-tax recovery, three statutory levers operate: the special method approval route at regulation 102 (verbatim heading 'Use of other methods', prior HMRC approval required, written method, fair-and-reasonable declaration); the standard-method override at regulation 107A (verbatim heading 'Adjustment of attribution', inserted by SI 2002/1074 effective 18 April 2002, triggered where standard-method attribution differs substantially from actual use); and the HMRC direction route at regulation 102B (where HMRC requires a taxable person to use a special method). This page walks each route in depth, classifies the typical Proposed Special Methods (PESMs) approved for property portfolios (sectorised, floor-area, headcount, transaction-count), runs the Lansdowne Estates worked example showing a 12-percentage-point recovery uplift on a £400,000 residual cost base, and closes with the decision tree mapping portfolio shape to method choice. Companion to our standard-method page; the special-method route is what comes after standard method when standard method does not work."
- Before: answer: "SI 1995/2518 regulation 107A (verbatim heading 'Adjustment of attribution') is the standard-method override provision, inserted by SI 2002/1074 (The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2002) effective 18 April 2002. (House position §29.6 was originally locked citing SI 2002/1142 as the inserting instrument; the verified citation is SI 2002/1074.) The override operates where the taxable person uses the standard method under regulation 101 but the attribution produced by that method 'differs substantially' from actual use of the goods or services in making taxable supplies. The provision requires the taxable person to account for the adjustment in the next prescribed accounting period after the longer period to which the adjustment relates. The override is taxpayer-initiated and self-assessed; HMRC does not need to direct it. Where the standard-method attribution materially over-recovers (relative to actual use), the override requires the taxpayer to repay the excess; where it materially under-recovers, additional recovery is claimable. The 'differs substantially' test is not numerically defined in regulation 107A; HMRC guidance suggests differences of a few percentage points or more on residual input tax of material size."
  After: answer: "SI 1995/2518 regulation 107A (verbatim heading 'Adjustment of attribution') is the standard-method override provision, inserted by SI 2002/1074 (The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2002) effective 18 April 2002. The override operates where the taxable person uses the standard method under regulation 101 but the attribution produced by that method 'differs substantially' from actual use of the goods or services in making taxable supplies. The provision requires the taxable person to account for the adjustment in the next prescribed accounting period after the longer period to which the adjustment relates. The override is taxpayer-initiated and self-assessed; HMRC does not need to direct it. Where the standard-method attribution materially over-recovers (relative to actual use), the override requires the taxpayer to repay the excess; where it materially under-recovers, additional recovery is claimable. The 'differs substantially' test is not numerically defined in regulation 107A; HMRC guidance suggests differences of a few percentage points or more on residual input tax of material size."

The option-to-tax framework (where opting changes the supply-status of commercial property and therefore the supply-value ratio that drives both standard and special methods) is the C1 PILLAR. This page sits within the cluster as the post-standard-method route depth."

- Before: answer: "Yes. For 2025/26 the annual allowance is £60,000, tapering by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 (where threshold income also exceeds £200,000) down to a £10,000 floor. For a defined-benefit scheme like the NHS Pension Scheme the measure is the pension input amount (capitalised growth), not contributions paid. A specialist firm models your input amount, applies carry-forward from the previous three years and, where a charge arises, advises on Scheme Pays. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance (£268,275) and Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance (£1,073,100)."
  After: answer: "Yes. For 2025/26 the annual allowance is £60,000, tapering by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 (where threshold income also exceeds £200,000) down to a £10,000 floor. For a defined-benefit scheme like the NHS Pension Scheme the measure is the pension input amount (capitalised growth), not contributions paid. Our medical accountants model your input amount, applies carry-forward from the previous three years and, where a charge arises, advises on Scheme Pays. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance (£268,275) and Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance (£1,073,100)."
- Before: answer: "Modern cloud accounting means you can work with a medical specialist regardless of location, and the firms we match enquiries to work with doctors across Merseyside and the wider North West. Sector expertise (NHS pension, GP partnership tax, locum status, private-practice planning) is far more valuable than a local high-street office. Choose on medical specialism first."
  After: answer: "Modern cloud accounting means you can work with a medical specialist regardless of location, and our team works with doctors across Merseyside and the wider North West. Sector expertise (NHS pension, GP partnership tax, locum status, private-practice planning) is far more valuable than a local high-street office. Choose on medical specialism first."
- Before: Whether you are a GP partner working out your share of practice profit, a salaried GP, a locum doctor weighing self-employment against a company, or a consultant managing mixed NHS and private earnings, you want an accountant who works with doctors every day. We are not that accountant: we publish the research and match enquiries to a regulated firm in our specialist partner network. This page sets out what specialist support for medical professionals across Liverpool and Merseyside actually covers, with the headline figures stated at 2026/27 rates and tagged to their tax year. It is general information, not personal advice.
  After: Whether you are a GP partner working out your share of practice profit, a salaried GP, a locum doctor weighing self-employment against a company, or a consultant managing mixed NHS and private earnings, you want an accountant who works with doctors every day. It is general information, not personal advice.
- Before: A specialist firm prepares the partnership accounts and the partnership return (SA800), and the individual returns for each partner, with the profit share flowing through to the partnership pages (SA104) of the personal return. A GP partner is taxed on their profit share, not their drawings , and pays Class 4 National Insurance on that trading profit (6% on profits from £12,570 to £50,270, then 2% above, for 2026/27). Class 2 has not been a required payment since 6 April 2024. For the full picture, see our GP partnership tax guide and our note on profit-sharing tax planning .
  After: Our medical accountants prepare the partnership accounts and the partnership return (SA800), and the individual returns for each partner, with the profit share flowing through to the partnership pages (SA104) of the personal return. A GP partner is taxed on their profit share, not their drawings , and pays Class 4 National Insurance on that trading profit (6% on profits from £12,570 to £50,270, then 2% above, for 2026/27). Class 2 has not been a required payment since 6 April 2024. For the full picture, see our GP partnership tax guide and our note on profit-sharing tax planning .
- Before: For more on what specialist support involves, see our complete guide to GP accountant services and our note on what UK medical professionals pay for a GP accountant . Monitoring pension growth against the £60,000 annual allowance (2025/26) and watching for the tapered allowance , which bites where threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000 , reducing the allowance by £1 for every £2 over £260,000 down to a £10,000 floor. Consultants and high-earning GPs are most exposed. Where a charge arises, a Scheme Pays election can settle it; see our Scheme Pays deadlines guide and the annual allowance guide .

Monitoring pension growth against the £60,000 annual allowance (2026/27) and watching for the tapered allowance , which bites where threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000 , reducing the allowance by £1 for every £2 over £260,000 down to a £10,000 floor. Consultants and high-earning GPs are most exposed. Where a charge arises, a Scheme Pays election can settle it; see our Scheme Pays deadlines guide and the annual allowance guide .
- Before: The single most valuable thing a medical accountant does is connect your tax position to your NHS Pension. That means tracking pension input against the £60,000 allowance (2025/26), spotting the taper early, advising on Scheme Pays where a charge arises (a 2025/26 charge must be elected by 31 July 2027), and timing income to reduce the impact of the tapered allowance. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance (£268,275) and the Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance (£1,073,100), so planning now centres on the annual allowance and lump-sum limits rather than a lifetime cap. The 2023 increase in the standard annual allowance from £40,000 to £60,000 is the historical change behind today's figures.
  After: The single most valuable thing a medical accountant does is connect your tax position to your NHS Pension. That means tracking pension input against the £60,000 allowance (2026/27), spotting the taper early, advising on Scheme Pays where a charge arises (a 2025/26 charge must be elected by 31 July 2027), and timing income to reduce the impact of the tapered allowance. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance (£268,275) and the Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance (£1,073,100), so planning now centres on the annual allowance and lump-sum limits rather than a lifetime cap. The 2023 increase in the standard annual allowance from £40,000 to £60,000 is the historical change behind today's figures.
**Medical/web/content/blog/accountant-self-assessment.md**

- Before: One medical point that often surfaces on the return is the NHS pension annual allowance charge . The annual allowance is £60,000 for 2025/26, tapering for very high earners, and it is measured on the growth in your pension (the pension input amount), not the contributions you pay. If your input amount exceeds your available allowance, the excess is taxed at your marginal rate and reported on your Self Assessment return. Where the charge is large enough you may be able to ask the NHS scheme to settle it under Scheme Pays rather than paying it personally. These are specialist calculations, covered in the annual allowance and Scheme Pays guides below.
  After: One medical point that often surfaces on the return is the NHS pension annual allowance charge . The annual allowance is £60,000 for 2026/27, tapering for very high earners, and it is measured on the growth in your pension (the pension input amount), not the contributions you pay. If your input amount exceeds your available allowance, the excess is taxed at your marginal rate and reported on your Self Assessment return.   After: NHS pension annual allowance of £60,000 (2026/27), tapered for high earners where threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000, down to a £10,000 floor
- Before: The NHS pension scheme is the most complex part of GP financial planning. The standard annual allowance is £60,000 (2025/26), tapering where threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000, reducing by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 to a minimum of £10,000. For a defined-benefit scheme the measure is the pension input amount (capitalised growth), not contributions paid. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance of £268,275 and the Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance of £1,073,100. High-earning Glasgow GP partners and consultants who breach the allowance can often settle the charge through Scheme Pays . See our NHS pension annual allowance guide and our explainer on minimising NHS pension tax charges .
  After: The NHS pension scheme is the most complex part of GP financial planning. The standard annual allowance is £60,000 (2026/27), tapering where threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000, reducing by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 to a minimum of £10,000. For a defined-benefit scheme the measure is the pension input amount (capitalised growth), not contributions paid. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and replaced by the Lump Sum Allowance of £268,275 and the Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance of £1,073,100. High-earning Glasgow GP partners and consultants who breach the allowance can often settle the charge through Scheme Pays . See our NHS pension annual allowance guide and our explainer on minimising NHS pension tax charges .

- Before: This is where many Liverpool GP partners are most exposed. For 2025/26 the annual allowance is £60,000 , tapering by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 (where threshold income also exceeds £200,000), down to a floor of £10,000 . Because the NHS Pension Scheme is a defined-benefit scheme, the charge is driven by the pension input amount (the capitalised growth in your benefits), not the contributions you pay, so a pay rise or a step up in pensionable profit can produce a large input amount in a single year. - Before: Capital gains and goodwill. A point unique to general practice: NHS GP goodwill cannot be sold , and has not been able to be since 1 April 2004 (now under SI 2019/251). So the dental-style "sell your goodwill and claim relief" approach does not apply to an NHS practice. A GP transaction is about tangible assets, owned premises and partnership capital accounts, plus any private goodwill, which is the only goodwill a GP can sell. Business Asset Disposal Relief applies only to a private-practice or private-company disposal and is charged at 18% for a disposal on or after 6 April 2026 (it was 14% from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026, and 10% before that). The CGT annual exempt amount is £3,000 for 2025/26. For the detail see whether GP practice goodwill can be sold and selling a private medical practice, CGT and BADR .

- Before: Building NHS pension as a locum has a tax dimension. The pension annual allowance is £60,000 (2025/26) . It tapers where your threshold income exceeds £200,000 and your adjusted income exceeds £260,000 , reducing by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000 down to a minimum of £10,000 . For a defined-benefit scheme the figure that is measured against the allowance is the pension input amount (the capitalised growth in your benefits), not the contributions you actually paid, so a locum with variable income can be surprised by a charge even when cash contributions look modest. Unused allowance can be carried forward from the previous three tax years.
  After: Building NHS pension as a locum has a tax dimension. The pension annual allowance is £60,000 (2026/27) . - Before: If you are an in-scheme member, your NHS pension annual allowance is £60,000 for 2025/26. It tapers where your threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000 , falling by £1 for every £2 of adjusted income above £260,000, down to a floor of £10,000. (These figures replaced the old £40,000 allowance, the £240,000 adjusted-income threshold and the £4,000 floor; the headline allowance rose from £40,000 to £60,000 back in April 2023.) The measure for a defined-benefit scheme is the growth in your pension's value (the pension input amount), not the contributions you pay. Private income on top of NHS pay is exactly what pushes high-earning doctors over the taper thresholds, so it is worth modelling before the year-end rather than discovering the charge afterwards. Our tapered annual allowance guide and the complete annual allowance guide work through this; if a charge does arise, see how Scheme Pays and its deadlines work .
  After: If you are an in-scheme member, your NHS pension annual allowance is £60,000 for 2026/27. (These figures replaced the old £40,000 allowance, the £240,000 adjusted-income threshold and the £4,000 floor; the headline allowance rose from £40,000 to £60,000 back in April 2023.) - Before: Most limited company agency founders take a salary up to the National Insurance primary threshold (£12,570 in 2025/26) to avoid both employee and employer NIC, while still qualifying for state pension entitlements. Remaining income is taken as dividends, which attract lower tax rates than salary: 8.75% (basic rate), 33.75% (higher rate) and 39.35% (additional rate) for the 2025/26 tax year.
  After: Most limited company agency founders take a salary up to the National Insurance primary threshold (£12,570 in 2026/27) to avoid both employee and employer NIC, while still qualifying for state pension entitlements. Remaining income is taken as dividends, which attract lower tax rates than salary: 10.75% (basic rate), 35.75% (higher rate) and 39.35% (additional rate) for the 2026/27 tax year.
- Before: Employer pension contributions from your limited company are one of the most tax-efficient ways to extract profit from your agency. Company contributions reduce corporation tax, avoid NIC entirely, and do not count as personal income. For higher-rate taxpayers, this can be significantly more efficient than dividends. The annual allowance is £60,000 (2025/26) across all pension contributions, including any personal contributions.
  After: Employer pension contributions from your limited company are one of the most tax-efficient ways to extract profit from your agency. Company contributions reduce corporation tax, avoid NIC entirely, and do not count as personal income. For higher-rate taxpayers, this can be significantly more efficient than dividends. - Before: "The turnover test compares your net CIS turnover (total CIS receipts minus VAT and materials) over the last 12 months against the threshold for your business structure. For a sole trader the threshold is £30,000. For a partnership it is £30,000 per partner OR £100,000 for the partnership as a whole. For a limited company it is £30,000 per director OR £100,000 in total. For a closely controlled company it is £30,000 per controller.   After: "The turnover test compares your net CIS turnover (total CIS receipts minus VAT and materials) over the last 12 months against the threshold for your business structure. For a sole trader the threshold is £30,000. For a partnership it is £30,000 per partner OR £100,000 for the partnership as a whole. For a limited company it is £30,000 per director OR £100,000 in total. For a closely controlled company it is £30,000 per controller. Net turnover is what matters: labour-only subcontractors find their net figure equals their gross CIS income, while those supplying significant materials may find their net turnover is considerably lower than their invoice total.",
- Before: "Finance Act 2026 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026, in force 6 April 2026) introduced a tougher GPS regime. **generalist/web/content/blog/invoice-finance-for-cleaning-companies.md**

- Before: Two tax points are worth flagging, though the mechanics sit one hop away with our tax guides rather than here. First, factoring service fees and discount margin are ordinary business finance costs and are generally deductible against your company's profits under the loan-relationship and finance-cost rules, which reduces the effective net cost of the facility. Second, because cleaning is so payroll-heavy, the real driver of your cash need is the fully loaded cost of employment, not just gross wages: employer National Insurance at 15% on earnings above the £5,000 secondary threshold (from April 2025), pension contributions and holiday pay all sit inside that 70% wage figure. Understanding the true cost of an employee in 2026/27 helps you size a facility to the payroll you are actually funding. For how finance costs interact with your corporation-tax position across the 19% to 25% rates and the 26.5% marginal band, see our corporation-tax marginal relief guide . If you want the structuring reviewed alongside the funding, our partner team can help; the finance introduction itself goes to the broker panel.

- Before: A client of ours runs a biotech startup in Manchester's Corridor district, developing a novel cell therapy for autoimmune disease. In their first year, they spent £63,400 on consumables. We helped them identify £47,200 of qualifying costs.
  After: Take a biotech startup developing a novel cell therapy for autoimmune disease. In their first year, they spend £63,400 on consumables, and a line-by-line review identifies £47,200 of qualifying costs.
- Before: The qualifying items included cell culture media (£8,400), custom antibodies (£12,600), PCR reagents and plasticware (£6,200), and third-party sequencing (£4,800). The remaining £15,200 was non-qualifying: general lab gloves, cleaning supplies, and equipment maintenance contracts.
  After: The qualifying items include cell culture media (£8,400), custom antibodies (£12,600), PCR reagents and plasticware (£6,200), and third-party sequencing (£4,800). The remaining £15,200 is non-qualifying: general lab gloves, cleaning supplies, and equipment maintenance contracts.
- Before: The £47,200 was included in their RDEC claim, generating a gross 20% expenditure credit of £9,440. Because RDEC is taxable income, the net cash benefit after corporation tax is approximately £7,080 at the 25% main rate (or £7,646 at the 19% small-profits rate). Without proper categorisation, they would have claimed the full £63,400 and risked an enquiry.
  After: The £47,200 is included in their RDEC claim, generating a gross 20% expenditure credit of £9,440. Because RDEC is taxable income, the net cash benefit after corporation tax is approximately £7,080 at the 25% main rate (or £7,646 at the 19% small-profits rate). - Before: Let's use a real example. A Manchester-based independent film company spends £400,000 on a qualifying British film. Core expenditure is £380,000, all of it in the UK. The additional deduction is £304,000 (80% of £380,000, which is lower than the £380,000 UK core spend). If the company has no other income, the loss created is £704,000 (the £400,000 actual spend plus the £304,000 additional deduction). Under the legacy FTR, the surrenderable loss is capped at the additional deduction. The payable credit is therefore £76,000 (25% of £304,000). That is a significant cash injection for a production company.
  After: Let's use a worked example. A Manchester-based independent film company spends £400,000 on a qualifying British film. Core expenditure is £380,000, all of it in the UK. The additional deduction is £304,000 (80% of £380,000, which is lower than the £380,000 UK core spend). If the company has no other income, the loss created is £704,000 (the £400,000 actual spend plus the £304,000 additional deduction). Under the legacy FTR, the surrenderable loss is capped at the additional deduction. The payable credit is therefore £76,000 (25% of £304,000). That is a significant cash injection for a production company.

- Before: Let me give you a real example. A director in Manchester runs a 2-employee software consultancy turning over £320,000. His personal tax bill for 2024/25 is £47,200. He asks his company to pay it directly from the business account. The company now has a director's loan of £47,200. At the year-end, the loan is still outstanding. The company files a P11D and pays Class 1A NIC on the notional benefit. Nine months after year-end, the loan is still unpaid. The company must pay S455 tax of £16,874 (35.75% of £47,200, the rate for loans made on or after 6 April 2026). The director now owes the company £47,200 plus the company has lost £16,874 in cash. That is a total of £64,074 tied up. Not a good outcome.

**generalist/web/content/blog/reconcile-directors-loan-account-year-end.md**

- Before: Here is a real example. Suppose you run a 4-employee software consultancy in Manchester turning over £420,000. You took £30,000 from the company in October to cover a personal tax bill. You intended to repay it within the year but forgot. At the 31 March year end, your DLA is overdrawn by £30,000. The company will owe £10,125 in S455 tax at the 33.75% rate that applied to loans made before 6 Apr 2026 (33.75% x £30,000). If the same loan were made on or after 6 Apr 2026 the charge rises to £10,725 (35.75% x £30,000). Either way, that is a significant cash flow hit.
  After: Here is a worked example. Suppose you run a 4-employee software consultancy in Manchester turning over £420,000. You took £30,000 from the company in October to cover a personal tax bill. You intended to repay it within the year but forgot. At the 31 March year end, your DLA is overdrawn by £30,000. The company will owe £10,125 in S455 tax at the 33.75% rate that applied to loans made before 6 Apr 2026 (33.75% x £30,000). If the same loan were made on or after 6 Apr 2026 the charge rises to £10,725 (35.75% x £30,000). Either way, that is a significant cash flow hit.

After the £3,000 annual CGT allowance, the taxable gain was £91,500. Tax at 18% (the BADR rate from 6 Apr 2026; 14% applied in 2025/26) was £16,470. The remaining directors paid nothing personally. The company's retained profits reduced to £85,000, but that was sufficient for working capital.
  After: The departing director's gain is £94,500 (after £500 base cost). BADR applies to the full gain because it is within the remaining £800,000 allowance. The company buyback saved them that cost.
  After: If the deal were structured as a personal purchase by the remaining directors, they would need to extract £95,000 as dividends first. **generalist/web/content/blog/when-do-you-need-property-tax-advisor.md**

- Before: Take a real example. A Manchester-based construction company owner owned a commercial unit personally that his company used. He wanted to sell it for £420,000. His base cost was £180,000. The gain of £240,000 would have attracted CGT at 24% as a higher-rate taxpayer: £57,600. With proper planning, we transferred the property into the company before sale using incorporation relief. The gain was deferred. The company then sold it and paid corporation tax at 19% on the gain, with the proceeds available for reinvestment without the immediate tax hit. That saved him roughly £12,000 in year one.
  After: Take a worked example. A Manchester-based construction company owner owned a commercial unit personally that his company used. He wanted to sell it for £420,000. His base cost was £180,000. The gain was deferred. The company then sold it and paid corporation tax at 19% on the gain, with the proceeds available for reinvestment without the immediate tax hit. That saved him roughly £12,000 in year one.

- Added: What we do
- Added: The problems that bring sellers to us repeat. The VAT threshold is measured on gross sales, not the payout the platform sends you, so a seller watching the bank balance can cross it without noticing. Deemed-supplier and establishment status decide whether the marketplace or you accounts for VAT on a sale. Overseas marketplace fees carry reverse-charge VAT that most bookkeeping misses. Sales into the EU bring IOSS and OSS obligations that sit under EU rather than UK law. And settlement reports mix revenue, fees, refunds and reserves in a way that has to be unpicked before the figures are fit for a VAT return or a set of accounts.
- Added: Our services are built around those problems:
- Added: VAT registration at the right time on the right scheme, ongoing VAT returns, and cross-border and marketplace VAT advice.
- Added: Monthly settlement and payout reconciliation that turns Amazon, eBay, Etsy and Shopify reports into gross trading figures, with cost of goods sold and inventory tracked properly.
- Added: EU VAT assessment for your selling pattern, IOSS intermediary coordination and ongoing EU compliance.
- Added: Self Assessment returns and limited company accounts, with owner extraction structured against current rates.
- Added: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax: digital records and quarterly updates for sole-trader sellers as the thresholds come down.
- Added: Responding to HMRC platform-reporting letters.
- Added: How an engagement starts
- Added: It starts with a conversation, not a proposal. You tell us what you sell, where you sell it and how the business is structured, through the enquiry form or by phone. One of our accountants calls you to go through it and answer the immediate questions, and that first call is free. If it makes sense to work together, we agree the scope before any work starts, so you know what is covered and what is not. From there we do the work, deal with HMRC on your behalf and keep you ahead of your deadlines.
- Added: Services run in three tiers, from self assessment essentials through VAT and reconciliation to full cross-border compliance, and you can move tier at any month-end. We reply to every enquiry within 24 hours.

**ecommerce/web/src/data/vat.ts**

- Before: body: " PVA works by moving the import VAT obligation from the border to your next VAT return. Instead of paying 20% of the customs value in cash at the port or airport and then waiting for the next return cycle to reclaim it, you declare the same amount in box 1 (output tax) and box 4 (input tax) of your VAT return. The cash difference is significant for a seller shipping large consignments: a £50,000 shipment of goods carries £10,000 of import VAT that PVA keeps in your business rather than in a HMRC float. HMRC issues a monthly postponed import VAT statement for each UK importer using PVA. This statement must reconcile to the boxes 1 and 4 entries on your return. If the statements are not being downloaded and reconciled each period, the return is unreconciled and a compliance risk. For generic importer PVA mechanics (customs declarations, commodity codes), see the generalist importing guide at Holloway Davies . ",
  After: body: " PVA works by moving the import VAT obligation from the border to your next VAT return. Instead of paying 20% of the customs value in cash at the port or airport and then waiting for the next return cycle to reclaim it, you declare the same amount in box 1 (output tax) and box 4 (input tax) of your VAT return. The cash difference is significant for a seller shipping large consignments: a £50,000 shipment of goods carries £10,000 of import VAT that PVA keeps in your business rather than in a HMRC float. HMRC issues a monthly postponed import VAT statement for each UK importer using PVA. This statement must reconcile to the boxes 1 and 4 entries on your return. If the statements are not being downloaded and reconciled each period, the return is unreconciled and a compliance risk. ",

**ecommerce/web/src/lib/calculators/tools/sole-trader-vs-ltd-sellers.ts**

- Before: answer: `At selling profits below roughly £30,000 to £35,000, the tax saving from incorporating rarely covers the extra accountancy fees. Above that level, a limited company can produce a lower tax bill, but only if profit is retained inside the company rather than fully extracted as salary and dividends. When every pound of profit is drawn out in the same year, the combined corporation tax plus dividend tax (at 10.75% basic rate from April 2026 under Finance Act 2026 s.4) exceeds the combined income tax and Class 4 NIC a sole trader pays in the basic band, so the sole trader stays ahead at full extraction. The company wins when you reinvest retained profits or leave them inside the business. The right answer depends on your profit level after platform fees and stock costs, how much you need to draw, any other income and your plans for the business. Use this calculator as a starting point and talk to an accountant before incorporating. For the generic version of this calculation without seller-specific inputs, the generalist incorporation calculator at hollowaydavies.co.uk covers that.`,
  After: answer: `At selling profits below roughly £30,000 to £35,000, the tax saving from incorporating rarely covers the extra accountancy fees. Above that level, a limited company can produce a lower tax bill, but only if profit is retained inside the company rather than fully extracted as salary and dividends. When every pound of profit is drawn out in the same year, the combined corporation tax plus dividend tax (at 10.75% basic rate from April 2026 under Finance Act 2026 s.4) exceeds the combined income tax and Class 4 NIC a sole trader pays in the basic band, so the sole trader stays ahead at full extraction. The company wins when you reinvest retained profits or leave them inside the business. The right answer depends on your profit level after platform fees and stock costs, how much you need to draw, any other income and your plans for the business. Use this calculator as a starting point and talk to an accountant before incorporating.`,
